title: What Is Base Salary? A Guide to Hourly Rates, the National Minimum Wage, and Award Pay
description: Understand what is base salary in Australia: how to calculate annual pay from an hourly rate, the National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, and superannuation.
salarySummary: For a 38-hour week, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, giving a base annual salary of $52,254.80 before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the minimum an award/agreement-free adult employee can be paid. Award rates are set by industry or occupation and are often higher. Most employees are covered by an award, which includes specific pay rates, penalties, and allowances. You can find your award rate using the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay Guides.

faqs.q: Does base salary include casual loading and superannuation?
faqs.a: No. Base salary (or base hourly rate) is the ordinary time rate before any loadings. Casual employees get a 25% loading on top of the base rate. Superannuation is paid on top of ordinary earnings at 12% (from 2026–27) and is not part of the base salary. Always check whether a quoted rate already includes loading.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by hours per week, then by 52. For a standard 38-hour week: hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual gross. For example, $30/hour × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. Use our [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) tool for quick estimates.

bodyMarkdown:
## What Is Base Salary?

When you see a job ad quoting an hourly rate or an annual salary, the number you need to start with is the **base salary** (or base hourly rate). This is the ordinary time rate for an employee before any loadings, penalties, allowances, or superannuation are added. Understanding what is base salary helps you compare job offers, check if you’re being paid correctly, and plan your budget.

In Australia, the base salary is almost always expressed as an hourly rate for award-covered employees or as an annual figure for salaried staff. The Fair Work Commission sets the [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) each year, and most industries have their own award rates that are higher. Knowing the difference is the first step to making sure you’re paid fairly.

### How to Calculate Annual Pay from an Hourly Rate

The standard formula used by the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian Taxation Office is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time employee working 38 ordinary hours per week (the standard under the National Employment Standards), the calculation is straightforward. For example:

- National Minimum Wage (from 1 July 2026): $26.44 per hour
- Weekly: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.90
- Fortnightly: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80
- Annual: $1,004.90 × 52 = $52,254.80

This matches the Fair Work Commission’s published figures. The same formula works for any hourly rate, but always check whether your award or agreement specifies a different ordinary hours span (some industries use 35 or 40 hours).

### National Minimum Wage vs. Award Rates

The National Minimum Wage is the legal floor. It applies to employees who are not covered by an award or registered agreement. However, the Fair Work Ombudsman notes that most employees are covered by an industry or occupation award, which sets higher minimum rates. For example, the Hospitality Award, the Retail Award, and the Clerks Award all have pay rates above the National Minimum Wage.

To find the correct base rate for your job, use the [pay guides](/blog) published by the Fair Work Ombudsman. These guides list minimum hourly rates for each classification in every award, plus allowances and penalty rates. If your employer pays you an annualised salary, they must ensure it covers at least what you would earn under the award for all hours worked, including penalties and overtime.

### Casual Loading and Superannuation

Two common additions to base salary are casual loading and superannuation. They are paid **on top** of the base rate.

- **Casual loading**: The National Minimum Wage Order 2026 specifies a 25% loading for casual employees. So a casual worker on the minimum wage gets $26.44 + 25% = $33.05 per hour. This compensates for not receiving paid leave. If you are casual, always confirm whether a quoted rate already includes the loading. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how to check.
- **Superannuation**: The Super Guarantee requires employers to pay 12% (from 2026–27) of ordinary earnings into your super fund. This is on top of your base salary. For example, on a $52,254.80 annual base, the super contribution would be about $6,270.58, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Super is not part of your take-home pay; it’s a separate retirement savings contribution.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Once you have your annual gross base salary, you can estimate tax using the 2026–27 resident rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus a Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). For a full-time worker on the National Minimum Wage ($52,254.80), the estimated tax is about $6,717 plus Medicare $1,045, leaving a take-home of roughly $44,493 per year, or $855 per week. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for a more precise estimate.

### Why the Fortnight Helps

Many employers pay fortnightly. Knowing your fortnightly base is useful for budgeting: just double the weekly amount. For the minimum wage, that’s $2,009.80 before tax and super. If you’re comparing a salary offer to an hourly rate, convert both to the same period. A $60,000 annual salary works out to $1,153.85 per week (÷52), or $30.36 per hour for a 38-hour week.

### When the Formula Doesn’t Apply

The simple hourly × 38 × 52 formula assumes you work the same hours every week with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. In reality, many employees receive shift penalties, overtime, or bonuses. If you have an annualised wage arrangement, your employer must review it each year to ensure it covers all award entitlements. Always check your payslip and keep a [timesheet](/).

### Summary

- **Base salary** is the ordinary time rate before loadings and super.
- Use **hourly rate × hours per week × 52** to get annual gross.
- The **National Minimum Wage** is $26.44/hour ($1,004.90/week) for 38 hours.
- **Award rates** are often higher; check the Fair Work Ombudsman’s pay guides.
- **Casual loading** (25%) and **super** (12%) are paid on top.
- **Tax** is calculated on gross income using the ATO’s 2026–27 brackets.

Understanding what is base salary puts you in control of your pay negotiations and helps you spot underpayment. For more detail, see our [reference tables](/data) and [average pay](/topics/average-pay) pages.
